title: T1021 — Remote Services
subtitle: Interactive walkthrough of Remote Services with the technique-specific attack path and defender evidence.
aria: Animated attack simulation: lateral movement with remote services

steps.title: Foothold and stolen credentials
steps.caption: The attacker already owns SALES-PC01 from a phishing email. A memory-reading tool pulls usernames and passwords out of lsass.exe, the Windows process that stores logon material. With credentials in hand, remote services are the next move.
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.

steps.title: Choose a way across the network
steps.caption: The attacker scans the local network for remote services. The file server answers on SMB 445, the domain controller on WinRM 5985, the Linux web server on SSH 22. Attackers pick whichever service is reachable and matches the credentials they hold.
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.

steps.title: SMB admin share to the file server
steps.caption: The attacker drops a small program into the file server's ADMIN$ share and installs it as a service. The service runs as SYSTEM, the machine's most powerful account. This is the classic PsExec path over SMB 445.
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.

steps.title: WinRM to the domain controller
steps.caption: Now the attacker opens PowerShell remoting (WinRM) to the domain controller with the stolen admin account. The logon shows up as a Type 3 network logon with the process name WSMAN. A backup-looking account is created to keep access.
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.

steps.title: SSH to the Linux server
steps.caption: The last target runs Linux, so the attacker switches to SSH with a stolen key file. Key logins need no password, so nothing fails or locks out. The only trace is one line in auth.log. They archive the /etc folder for later reading.
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.

steps.title: Collect and exfiltrate
steps.caption: The attacker copies the finance folder from the file server back to the workstation, then out to the internet. The traffic is normal SMB, but the volume, the account, and the hour all break the baseline pattern.
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.

steps.title: Blocked? Switch services
steps.caption: Security blocks RDP 3389 after an earlier alert, so the team thinks the attack is stopped. But SMB and WinRM are still open, so the attacker simply switches doors and reconnects. That is the core lesson of T1021: block one service, and the others carry the attack.
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.

steps.title: How defenders catch this
steps.caption: The SOC runs one cross-service query. One workstation made remote-service logons to four different servers in nine minutes, mixing SMB, WinRM, and SSH. No single-service rule could join that story; this one counts distinct servers per source, whatever the service.
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.
